\section{NLO cut masters and endpoint reconstruction}
\label{sec:nlo-example}

The NLO real-emission cut system is sufficiently small to solve analytically
without discarding its dependence on \(\eps\), its physical branches, or its
endpoint powers.  It provides a connected example of the reduction from
physical cuts to master integrals, differential equations, and
distributions in \(w\).  The calculation in this section determines the
complete NLO cut-master system.  It does not by itself constitute a complete
polarized NLO hard function.

\subsection{Two-particle cut and normalized master basis}
\label{subsec:nlo-two-particle-cut}

Let
\begin{equation}
 q:=k_a+k_b-k_c,
 \qquad
 Q^2:=q^2=s+t+u,
 \label{eq:nlo-recoil-momentum}
\end{equation}
with the invariants and physical chamber defined in
Eqs.~\eqref{eq:partonic-invariants} and \eqref{eq:physical-chamber}.
At NLO there is one independent real-emission momentum \(k\), while the
second cut momentum is \(q-k\).  The massless two-particle phase-space
measure is
\begin{equation}
 \dd\Phi_2(q;k,q-k)
 =
 (2\pi)^{2-D}\dd^Dk\,
 \delta_+(k^2)\,
 \delta_+\!\bigl((q-k)^2\bigr).
 \label{eq:nlo-two-body-measure}
\end{equation}

In the rest frame of \(q\),
\begin{equation}
 q^\mu=(\sqrt{Q^2},\boldsymbol 0),
 \qquad
 k^\mu=\frac{\sqrt{Q^2}}{2}(1,\widehat{\boldsymbol n}),
 \qquad
 \widehat{\boldsymbol n}^{\,2}=1.
 \label{eq:nlo-rest-frame-cut-momentum}
\end{equation}
Using
\begin{equation}
 \Omega_d
 =
 \frac{2\pi^{(d+1)/2}}{\Gamma((d+1)/2)}
 \label{eq:nlo-sphere-volume}
\end{equation}
for the volume of the unit \(d\)-sphere, integration of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-two-body-measure} gives
\begin{align}
 \Phi_2(Q^2,\eps)
 :={}&
 \int\dd\Phi_2(q;k,q-k)
 \notag\\
 ={}&
 (2\pi)^{2-D}
 \frac{\Omega_{D-2}}{2^{D-1}}
 (Q^2)^{D/2-2}
 \notag\\
 ={}&
 \frac{(4\pi)^\eps}{8\pi}
 \frac{\Gamma(1-\eps)}{\Gamma(2-2\eps)}
 (Q^2)^{-\eps}.
 \label{eq:nlo-two-body-volume}
\end{align}
No factor of \(\mu^{2\eps}\) is implicit in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-two-body-volume}.

It is useful to separate the common factor
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P_2(Q^2,\eps)
 :=
 \frac{(4\pi)^\eps\Gamma(1-\eps)}
      {16\pi^2\Gamma(1-2\eps)}
 (Q^2)^{-\eps},
 \qquad
 \Phi_2
 =
 \frac{2\pi}{1-2\eps}\mathcal P_2.
 \label{eq:nlo-reduced-phase-space-factor}
\end{equation}
The reduced cut bubble is therefore
\begin{equation}
 \widehat B(\eps)
 :=
 \mathcal P_2^{-1}
 \int\dd\Phi_2
 =
 \frac{2\pi}{1-2\eps}.
 \label{eq:nlo-bubble-result}
\end{equation}

For signs
\begin{equation}
 \sigma_i\in\{+1,-1\}
 \label{eq:nlo-momentum-flow-signs}
\end{equation}
and four-dimensional external vectors \(R_i\), define
\begin{equation}
 L_i(k):=\sigma_i k+R_i
 \label{eq:nlo-linear-line-momentum}
\end{equation}
and the reduced top integral
\begin{equation}
 \widehat T[\sigma_1,R_1;\sigma_2,R_2]
 :=
 \mathcal P_2^{-1}
 \int\dd\Phi_2\,
 \frac{1}{L_1(k)^2L_2(k)^2}.
 \label{eq:nlo-top-definition}
\end{equation}
The signs \(\sigma_i\) describe momentum flow and are not causal signs.

For the five NLO tops below, each ordinary denominator has a fixed sign in
the open physical phase space and can vanish only on a soft or collinear
boundary.  The complete dimensionally regulated terms possess a convergence
domain in which these boundary singularities define meromorphic integrals.
Equation~\eqref{eq:nlo-top-definition} consequently denotes that
prescription-independent meromorphic family.  This statement is not a
pointwise identification of the \(+i0\) and \(-i0\) distributions at their
boundary zeros.

The six physical masters are the bubble
\(\widehat B\) and
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  \widehat T_{ac}
  &=
  \widehat T[-1,k_a;+1,k_c],
  &
  \widehat T_{ab}
  &=
  \widehat T[-1,k_a;-1,k_b],
  \\[1mm]
  \widehat T_{abb}
  &=
  \widehat T[-1,k_a;-1,k_a-k_c],
  &
  \widehat T_{cb}
  &=
  \widehat T[+1,k_c;-1,k_b],
  \\[1mm]
  \widehat T_{cbb}
  &=
  \widehat T[+1,k_c;-1,k_a-k_c].
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:nlo-five-top-masters}
\end{equation}
For example,
\[
 \widehat T_{ac}
 \propto
 \frac{1}{(k_a-k)^2(k_c+k)^2},
 \qquad
 \widehat T_{abb}
 \propto
 \frac{1}{(k_a-k)^2(k_a-k_c-k)^2},
\]
which fixes the momentum-flow convention unambiguously.

The six masters form three powered-integral equivalence classes and three
positive-denominator equivalence classes.  One class contains only the two
physical cuts, while two nontrivial denominator classes are maximal under
denominator inclusion:
\begin{equation}
 N_{\rm master}^{\rm NLO}=6,
 \qquad
 N_{\rm pow}^{\rm NLO}=3,
 \qquad
 N_{\rm den}^{\rm NLO}=3,
 \qquad
 N_{\rm max}^{\rm NLO}=2.
 \label{eq:nlo-class-counts}
\end{equation}
These geometric counts do not determine the number of independent boundary
constants.

\subsection{One generic angular integral}
\label{subsec:nlo-generic-top}

For the line momentum in Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-linear-line-momentum}, define the
signed scale and its Gram discriminant by
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda_i
 :=
 R_i^2+\sigma_i q\cdot R_i,
 \qquad
 \Delta_i
 :=
 (q\cdot R_i)^2-Q^2R_i^2.
 \label{eq:nlo-lambda-delta}
\end{equation}
For every line in Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-five-top-masters}, either
\begin{equation}
 R_i^2=0
 \qquad\text{or}\qquad
 (q+\sigma_iR_i)^2=0.
 \label{eq:nlo-null-line-condition}
\end{equation}
It follows that
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_i=\Lambda_i^2.
 \label{eq:nlo-degenerate-gram-condition}
\end{equation}
The quantities \(\Lambda_i\) retain their signs; no absolute value is taken.

In the rest frame of \(q\), define the Euclidean unit vectors
\begin{equation}
 \boldsymbol e_i
 :=
 \frac{\sigma_i\sqrt{Q^2}\,\boldsymbol R_i}{\Lambda_i},
 \qquad
 \boldsymbol e_i^{\,2}=1.
 \label{eq:nlo-angular-unit-vectors}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 L_i(k)^2
 =
 \Lambda_i
 \bigl(1-\widehat{\boldsymbol n}\cdot\boldsymbol e_i\bigr).
 \label{eq:nlo-angular-denominator}
\end{equation}
The relative angle is
\begin{equation}
 \chi_{12}
 :=
 \boldsymbol e_1\cdot\boldsymbol e_2
 =
 \sigma_1\sigma_2
 \frac{
  (q\cdot R_1)(q\cdot R_2)
  -Q^2R_1\cdot R_2
 }{
  \Lambda_1\Lambda_2
 },
 \label{eq:nlo-angular-cosine}
\end{equation}
and the single cross ratio is
\begin{equation}
 z:=\frac{1+\chi_{12}}{2}.
 \label{eq:nlo-cross-ratio}
\end{equation}

After integrating the transverse angles and introducing a stereographic
coordinate \(y\), the reduced bubble and top become
\begin{align}
 \widehat B(\eps)
 &=
 \frac{2\pi}{1-2\eps},
 \notag\\
 \widehat T(z,\eps;\Lambda_1,\Lambda_2)
 &=
 \frac{\pi}{\Lambda_1\Lambda_2}
 \int_0^\infty
 \dd y\,
 \frac{(1+y)^\eps}{1+(1-z)y}
 \notag\\
 &=
 -\frac{\pi}
 {\eps\Lambda_1\Lambda_2}
 {}_2F_1(1,1;1-\eps;z).
 \label{eq:nlo-generic-top}
\end{align}
The Euler integral converges for
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Re}\eps<0.
 \label{eq:nlo-top-convergence-domain}
\end{equation}
For \(0<z<1\),
\begin{equation}
 1+(1-z)y>0
 \qquad
 (y\geq0),
 \label{eq:nlo-top-positive-base}
\end{equation}
so Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-generic-top} defines a real branch in the convergence
domain before meromorphic continuation in \(\eps\).

The five physical top masters are obtained from this one function by the
substitutions in Table~\ref{tab:nlo-top-maps}.
\begin{table}[htbp]
 \centering
 \small
 \begin{tabular}{@{}ccl@{}}
  \toprule
  Integral
  &
  \(z_\alpha\)
  &
  \((\Lambda_{\alpha,1},\Lambda_{\alpha,2})\)
  \\
  \midrule
  \(\widehat T_{ac}\)
  &
  \(\displaystyle\frac{su}{(s+t)(t+u)}\)
  &
  \(\displaystyle
   \left(
    -\frac{s+t}{2},
    -\frac{t+u}{2}
   \right)\)
  \\[2mm]
  \(\widehat T_{ab}\)
  &
  \(\displaystyle\frac{tu}{(s+t)(s+u)}\)
  &
  \(\displaystyle
   \left(
    -\frac{s+t}{2},
    -\frac{s+u}{2}
   \right)\)
  \\[2mm]
  \(\widehat T_{abb}\)
  &
  \(\displaystyle\frac{sQ^2}{(s+t)(s+u)}\)
  &
  \(\displaystyle

  &

\end{table}

The physical interval follows from
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  1-z_{ac}
  &=
  \frac{tQ^2}{(s+t)(t+u)},
  &
  1-z_{ab}
  &=
  \frac{sQ^2}{(s+t)(s+u)},
  \\[1mm]
  1-z_{abb}
  &=
  \frac{tu}{(s+t)(s+u)},
  &
  1-z_{cb}
  &=
  \frac{uQ^2}{(s+u)(t+u)},
  \\[1mm]
  1-z_{cbb}
  &=
  \frac{st}{(s+u)(t+u)}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:nlo-one-minus-cross-ratios}
\end{equation}
In the chamber of Eq.~\eqref{eq:physical-chamber}, both
\(z_\alpha\) and \(1-z_\alpha\) are positive.  Hence
\begin{equation}
 0<z_\alpha<1
 \qquad
 \text{for every }
 \alpha\in\{ac,ab,abb,cb,cbb\}.
 \label{eq:nlo-physical-cross-ratio-range}
\end{equation}

\subsection{Angular IBP, differential equation, and physical solution}
\label{subsec:nlo-differential-equation}

Normalize the bubble to unity and remove the two signed propagator scales:
\begin{equation}
 b(\eps)
 :=
 \frac{1-2\eps}{2\pi}\widehat B(\eps)
 =1,
 \qquad
 h(z,\eps)
 :=
 \frac{\Lambda_1\Lambda_2}{\pi}
 \widehat T(z,\eps;\Lambda_1,\Lambda_2).
 \label{eq:nlo-normalized-bubble-top}
\end{equation}
With
\begin{equation}
 \tau:=\frac{y}{1+y},
 \qquad
 y=\frac{\tau}{1-\tau},
 \label{eq:nlo-euler-variable}
\end{equation}
the top integral becomes
\begin{equation}
 h(z,\eps)
 =
 \int_0^1
 \frac{
  \dd\tau\,
  (1-\tau)^{-1-\eps}
 }{
  1-z\tau
 },
 \qquad
 0<z<1,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Re}\eps<0.
 \label{eq:nlo-euler-integral}
\end{equation}

Define
\begin{equation}
 g(\tau)
 :=
 \frac{\tau(1-\tau)^{-\eps}}{1-z\tau}.
 \label{eq:nlo-angular-ibp-vector}
\end{equation}
For \(\operatorname{Re}\eps<0\),
\begin{equation}
 g(0)=g(1)=0.
 \label{eq:nlo-angular-boundary-vanishing}
\end{equation}
The pointwise identity
\begin{align}
 -z\frac{\dd g}{\dd\tau}
 ={}&
 z(1-z)
 \frac{\partial}{\partial z}
 \left[
  \frac{(1-\tau)^{-1-\eps}}{1-z\tau}
 \right]
 \notag\\
 &-
 (z+\eps)
 \frac{(1-\tau)^{-1-\eps}}{1-z\tau}
 +
 \eps(1-\tau)^{-1-\eps}
 \label{eq:nlo-angular-ibp-identity}
\end{align}
and
\begin{equation}
 \int_0^1
 \dd\tau\,
 (1-\tau)^{-1-\eps}
 =
 -\frac{1}{\eps}
 \label{eq:nlo-lower-angular-integral}
\end{equation}
give
\begin{equation}
 z(1-z)\frac{\partial h}{\partial z}
 -(z+\eps)h
 =
 b.
 \label{eq:nlo-top-first-order}
\end{equation}
Together with \(\partial_z b=0\), this is the triangular system
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\partial}{\partial z}
 \begin{pmatrix}
  b\\ h
 \end{pmatrix}
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
  0&0\\[1mm]
  \dfrac{1}{z(1-z)}
  &
  \dfrac{z+\eps}{z(1-z)}
 \end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}
  b\\ h
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \label{eq:nlo-triangular-system}
\end{equation}

The integrating factor is
\begin{equation}
 \mu(z)
 =
 z^{-\eps}(1-z)^{1+\eps},
 \label{eq:nlo-integrating-factor}
\end{equation}
and Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-top-first-order} becomes
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\dd}{\dd z}
 \bigl[\mu(z)h(z,\eps)\bigr]
 =
 b\,z^{-1-\eps}(1-z)^\eps.
 \label{eq:nlo-integrating-factor-equation}
\end{equation}
The general solution is therefore
\begin{equation}
 h(z,\eps)
 =
 z^\eps(1-z)^{-1-\eps}
 \left[
  C(\eps)
  +
  b
  \int_0^z
  \dd\xi\,
  \xi^{-1-\eps}(1-\xi)^\eps
 \right].
 \label{eq:nlo-general-de-solution}
\end{equation}

In the convergence domain,
Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-euler-integral} has the finite limit
\begin{equation}
 h(0,\eps)
 =
 \int_0^1
 \dd\tau\,
 (1-\tau)^{-1-\eps}
 =
 -\frac{b}{\eps}.
 \label{eq:nlo-z0-boundary-value}
\end{equation}
The homogeneous term behaves as
\begin{equation}
 C(\eps)z^\eps
 \qquad
 (z\to0^+),
 \label{eq:nlo-z0-homogeneous-mode}
\end{equation}
which diverges for \(\operatorname{Re}\eps<0\) unless
\begin{equation}
 C(\eps)=0.
 \label{eq:nlo-regularity-condition}
\end{equation}
The physical solution is consequently
\begin{align}
 h(z,\eps)
 &=
 z^\eps(1-z)^{-1-\eps}
 B_z(-\eps,1+\eps)
 \notag\\
 &=
 -\frac{1}{\eps}
 {}_2F_1(1,1;1-\eps;z).
 \label{eq:nlo-physical-de-solution}
\end{align}
The boundary condition is imposed before meromorphic continuation in
\(\eps\).

For completeness, the residue matrices of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-triangular-system} are
\begin{equation}
 R_0
 :=
 \lim_{z\to0}
 zA(z,\eps)
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
  0&0\\
  1&\eps
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{spec}(R_0)=\{0,\eps\},
 \label{eq:nlo-z0-residue}
\end{equation}
and, with \(\rho:=1-z\),
\begin{equation}
 R_1
 :=
 \lim_{\rho\to0}
 \rho[-A(1-\rho,\eps)]
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
  0&0\\
  -1&-1-\eps
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{spec}(R_1)=\{0,-1-\eps\}.
 \label{eq:nlo-z1-residue}
\end{equation}
At \(z=0\), convenient eigenvectors are
\begin{equation}
 \begin{pmatrix}1\\-1/\eps\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix},
 \label{eq:nlo-z0-eigenvectors}
\end{equation}
for exponents \(0\) and \(\eps\), respectively.  The physical cycle selects
the first.  At \(z=1\), the regular and singular eigenvectors may be chosen
as
\begin{equation}
 \begin{pmatrix}1\\-1/(1+\eps)\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix},
 \label{eq:nlo-z1-eigenvectors}
\end{equation}
with exponents \(0\) and \(-1-\eps\).

Eliminating \(b\) gives the second-order equation for
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal F(z,\eps):=-\eps h(z,\eps),
 \label{eq:nlo-hypergeometric-function}
\end{equation}
namely
\begin{equation}
 z(1-z)\mathcal F''
 +(1-\eps-3z)\mathcal F'
 -\mathcal F
 =
 0.
 \label{eq:nlo-hypergeometric-equation}
\end{equation}

The exact connection formula between the two endpoints is
\begin{align}
 h(z,\eps)
 ={}&
 -\frac{1}{1+\eps}
 {}_2F_1(1,1;2+\eps;1-z)
 \notag\\
 &-
 \frac{\Gamma(1-\eps)\Gamma(1+\eps)}{\eps}
 z^\eps(1-z)^{-1-\eps}.
 \label{eq:nlo-connection-formula}
\end{align}
For \(0<z<1\), both \(z\) and \(1-z\) are positive and all powers in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-connection-formula} use real logarithms.  The formula
therefore separates the regular and singular \(z\to1^-\) branches without
an additional power identity.

The differential-equation count is now unambiguous.  Up to the exact
kinematic substitutions in Table~\ref{tab:nlo-top-maps}, the six physical
masters require one distinct triangular bubble--top system.  Its general
solution contains two formal constants: the bubble normalization \(b\) and
the homogeneous top coefficient \(C(\eps)\).  Physical regularity sets
\(C(\eps)=0\), while the elementary two-particle phase-space integral fixes
\(b=1\).  The top endpoint
\[
 h(0,\eps)=-\frac{1}{\eps}
\]
then follows from the same local solution and is not an additional
independent period.  Thus
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \begin{aligned}
  N_{\rm master}^{\rm NLO}&=6,
  \\
  N_{\rm DE,\ distinct}^{\rm NLO}&=1,
  \\
  N_{\rm boundary,\ independent}^{\rm NLO}&=1,
  \\
  N_{\rm boundary,\ non\text{-}elementary}^{\rm NLO}&=0.
 \end{aligned}
 }
 \label{eq:nlo-boundary-count}
\end{equation}
The nontrivial hypergeometric dependence is generated by transport in \(z\);
it is not supplied by a non-elementary boundary integration.

\subsection{Pullback to the real-emission endpoint}
\label{subsec:nlo-endpoint-pullback}

Use the variables of Eq.~\eqref{eq:vw-definitions},
\begin{equation}
 t=-s(1-v),
 \qquad
 u=-sv(1-x),
 \qquad
 Q^2=svx,
 \qquad
 x=1-w.
 \label{eq:nlo-vwx-map}
\end{equation}
At fixed \(0<v<1\), the endpoint is
\begin{equation}
 x\longrightarrow0^+.
 \label{eq:nlo-x-endpoint}
\end{equation}
The five cross ratios become
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  z_{ac}(x)
  &=
  \frac{1-x}{1-vx},
  &
  z_{ab}(x)
  &=
  \frac{(1-v)(1-x)}{1-v+vx},
  &
  z_{abb}(x)
  &=
  \frac{x}{1-v+vx},
  \\[1mm]
  z_{cb}(x)
  &=
  \frac{1-v}
  {(1-v+vx)(1-vx)},
  &
  z_{cbb}(x)
  &=
  \frac{v^2x(1-x)}
  {(1-v+vx)(1-vx)}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:nlo-cross-ratios-endpoint}
\end{equation}
Their exact endpoint factors are
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  1-z_{ac}
  &=
  \frac{(1-v)x}{1-vx},
  &
  1-z_{ab}
  &=
  \frac{x}{1-v+vx},
  &
  z_{abb}
  &=
  \frac{x}{1-v+vx},
  \\[1mm]
  1-z_{cb}
  &=
  \frac{v^2x(1-x)}
  {(1-v+vx)(1-vx)},
  &
  z_{cbb}
  &=
  \frac{v^2x(1-x)}
  {(1-v+vx)(1-vx)}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:nlo-cross-ratio-endpoint-factors}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 z_{ac},z_{ab},z_{cb}\longrightarrow1^-,
 \qquad
 z_{abb},z_{cbb}\longrightarrow0^+.
 \label{eq:nlo-cross-ratio-endpoint-directions}
\end{equation}

The common phase-space factor is
\begin{equation}
 (Q^2)^{-\eps}
 =
 (sv)^{-\eps}x^{-\eps}.
 \label{eq:nlo-phase-space-endpoint-factor}
\end{equation}
The signed scales in Table~\ref{tab:nlo-top-maps} remain finite and nonzero
at \(x=0\); they change endpoint coefficients but not endpoint exponents.

For the two masters approaching \(z=0\),
Eq.~\eqref{eq:nlo-z0-boundary-value} gives
\begin{equation}
 x^{-\eps}h(z_\alpha(x),\eps)
 =
 -\frac{x^{-\eps}}{\eps}
 +
 O\!\left(x^{1-\eps}\right),
 \qquad
 \alpha\in\{abb,cbb\}.
 \label{eq:nlo-z0-pulled-back-solution}
\end{equation}
For the three masters approaching \(z=1\), define
\begin{equation}
 c_{ac}=1-v,
 \qquad
 c_{ab}=\frac{1}{1-v},
 \qquad
 c_{cb}=\frac{v^2}{1-v}.
 \label{eq:nlo-z1-linear-coefficients}
\end{equation}
Since
\begin{equation}
 1-z_\alpha(x)
 =
 c_\alpha x+O(x^2),
 \qquad
 \alpha\in\{ac,ab,cb\},
 \label{eq:nlo-z1-linear-approach}
\end{equation}
the connection formula gives
\begin{align}
 x^{-\eps}h(z_\alpha(x),\eps)
 ={}&
 -\frac{x^{-\eps}}{1+\eps}
 \bigl[1+O(x)\bigr]
 \notag\\
 &-
 \frac{\Gamma(1-\eps)\Gamma(1+\eps)}{\eps}
 c_\alpha^{-1-\eps}
 x^{-1-2\eps}
 \bigl[1+O(x)\bigr].
 \label{eq:nlo-z1-pulled-back-solution}
\end{align}
Together with the bubble, the individual normalized masters therefore
contain only the noninteger endpoint modes
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 x^{-\eps},
 \qquad
 x^{-1-2\eps}.
 }
 \label{eq:nlo-individual-master-modes}
\end{equation}

These modes must be distinguished from the endpoint powers of the complete
hard-scattering coefficient.  If a rational coefficient has the local
valuation
\begin{equation}
 r_i(v,x,\eps)
 =
 x^{n_i}
 \bigl[
  r_i^{(0)}(v,\eps)+O(x)
 \bigr],
 \qquad
 n_i\in\mathbb Z,
 \qquad
 r_i^{(0)}\neq0,
 \label{eq:nlo-rational-endpoint-valuation}
\end{equation}
it shifts only the integer part of the corresponding master exponent.

For the complete singular real-emission coefficient, the regular master
branch is multiplied by an overall \(x^{-1}\) rational factor, while the
coefficient of the singular \(x^{-1-2\eps}\) branch is finite at \(x=0\).
The two endpoint sectors are therefore
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_{\rm sing}(v,x,\eps)
 =
 C_1(v,\eps)x^{-1-\eps}
 +
 C_2(v,\eps)x^{-1-2\eps}.
 \label{eq:nlo-two-endpoint-branches}
\end{equation}
The first sector is not an additional master mode: it is the
\(x^{-\eps}\) master branch multiplied by an integer pole \(x^{-1}\).
Both sectors must be retained until the complete projected coefficient has
been assembled; a cancellation in a restricted subset of diagrams does not
remove either allowed branch from the full analysis.

Using \(x=1-w\) and the distribution identity
Eq.~\eqref{eq:endpoint-distribution-identity}, one obtains the exact series
\begin{align}
 \mathcal R_{\rm sing}
 ={}&
 -\delta(1-w)
 \left[
  \frac{C_1(v,\eps)}{\eps}
  +
  \frac{C_2(v,\eps)}{2\eps}
 \right]
 \notag\\
 &+
 \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}
 \frac{(-\eps)^m}{m!}
 \left[
  C_1(v,\eps)
  +
  2^m C_2(v,\eps)
 \right]
 \mathcal D_m(w).
 \label{eq:nlo-two-branch-distribution}
\end{align}
The first terms are
\begin{align}
 \mathcal R_{\rm sing}
 ={}&
 -\delta(1-w)
 \left[
  \frac{C_1}{\eps}
  +
  \frac{C_2}{2\eps}
 \right]
 +(C_1+C_2)\mathcal D_0(w)
 \notag\\
 &-
 \eps(C_1+2C_2)\mathcal D_1(w)
 +
 \frac{\eps^2}{2}
 (C_1+4C_2)\mathcal D_2(w)
 +\cdots ,
 \label{eq:nlo-two-branch-distribution-first-terms}
\end{align}
where the arguments \((v,\eps)\) of \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are suppressed only
in the second equation.  Their Laurent expansions are inserted after the
exact endpoint branches have been converted to distributions.  In
particular, a \(1/\eps\) pole in either coefficient produces a
\(1/\eps^2\) contribution multiplying \(\delta(1-w)\).

\subsection{Scope of the unpolarized fixed-order comparison}
\label{subsec:nlo-uu-comparison}

The reverse-unitarity calculation above determines the real-emission cut
contribution.  To state precisely what has been compared with
Ref.~\cite{Aversa:1988vb}, define the singular projection at NLO by
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak S_{w=1}[F]
 :=
 F_\delta(v,\eps)\delta(1-w)
 +
 F_1(v,\eps)\mathcal D_1(w)
 +
 F_0(v,\eps)\mathcal D_0(w).
 \label{eq:nlo-singular-projection}
\end{equation}
In the normalization adopted for the unpolarized comparison,
\begin{align}
 \mathfrak S_{w=1}
 \bigl[
  H_{\mathsf{UU}}^{(1)}
 \bigr]
 ={}&
 \mathfrak S_{w=1}
 \bigl[
  H_{\mathsf{UU},\rm real}^{(1)}
 \bigr]
 +
 \mathfrak S_{w=1}
 \bigl[
  H_{\mathsf{UU},\rm virt+UV}^{(1)}
 \bigr]
 \notag\\
 &-
 \mathfrak S_{w=1}
 \bigl[
  H_{\mathsf{UU},\rm coll}^{(1)}
 \bigr],
 \label{eq:nlo-uu-assembly}
\end{align}
where \(H_{\rm coll}^{(1)}\) denotes the positive collinear convolution
kernel that is subtracted in the chosen factorization convention.

The exact comparison establishes
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  H_{\mathsf{UU},1}^{(1)}
  &=
  H_{\mathsf{UU},1}^{(1),\mathrm{Aversa}},
  \\
  H_{\mathsf{UU},0}^{(1)}
  &=
  H_{\mathsf{UU},0}^{(1),\mathrm{Aversa}},
  \\
  H_{\mathsf{UU},\delta}^{(1)}
  &=
  H_{\mathsf{UU},\delta}^{(1),\mathrm{Aversa}},
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:nlo-uu-singular-comparison}
\end{equation}
as exact analytic identities in the adopted normalization.  This verifies
the relative signs and normalization of the real, virtual-plus-UV, and
collinear terms for the three singular unpolarized coefficients.

Equation~\eqref{eq:nlo-uu-singular-comparison} does not establish the regular
\(w<1\) remainder, an LL fixed-order coefficient, a TT fixed-order
coefficient, or a complete polarized NLO hard function.  Those quantities
require their own real, virtual, ultraviolet-renormalization, and collinear
factorization calculations.
